name: Atomic Tangerine
lede: Atomic Tangerine is a bright peach-orange that Wikipedia lists among Crayola's crayon colors, though no source consulted here gives the year Crayola added it.

sections.title: A crayon name, undocumented beyond that
sections.body:
Our only sources for this color are Wikipedia, which names it as a Crayola color, and a Japanese traditional-color cross-reference to Umezome (梅染), meaning plum-dyed [1]. Neither explains why "atomic" was paired with "tangerine," and no book consulted here dates the pairing [1]. The classification here tags "Atomic" as a place or institution word, though that label describes how our system sorts the name rather than any documented origin [1].

The closest named color on screen is [[light-salmon]], 3.7 units away and read as duller than Atomic Tangerine; [[yellowish-cinnamon]] sits at the same distance, also duller, [[apricot-buff]] at 4.3, duller still, and [[orangeish]] at 4.4, more vivid [3]. A [[gem:coral|coral]] twin in our gems data sits further off, 6.4 units, a loose match at best [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This is a rare color in our painting archive: it appears in only 0.07 percent of 23,781 paintings, 16 of them, and the within-painting lens isolates it as a dominant area in 10, as photographed [2]. That ranks it rarer than 68 percent of the named colors we track [2]. Inside those 10 paintings it plays an accent 70 percent of the time, by lightness rank [2]. The earliest match in our archive is a 1470 painting by Sandro Botticelli, with only 9 dated matches overall, too thin to say when the look-alike hue first appears reliably, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. In printed English the word has risen fastest in the 2000s and peaked in the same decade, a sign this is a recent coinage rather than an old one (Google Books, all senses of the word) [2].
